name: Structure of the Nervous System
what: This subtopic covers the two major divisions of the nervous system — the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system — and their subdivisions, including the somatic nervous system, autonomic nervous system, sympathetic nervous system, and parasympathetic nervous system. It also covers the three types of neurons and the structures they make up.
why: Understanding the structure of the nervous system is the foundation for explaining how the body detects, processes, and responds to information. Every other concept in this chapter depends on knowing which division does what and where.

items.title: I can name the two major divisions of the nervous system and describe what each comprises
items.what: The central nervous system (CNS) comprises the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) comprises every neuron in the body outside the CNS. Together, these two divisions make up the entire nervous system.
items.why: Distinguishing between the CNS and PNS is essential for accurately describing the pathway of neural messages in both conscious and unconscious responses, and is tested directly in VCE exam questions.
items.example: When a person feels cold water on their hand, sensory receptors in the skin (PNS) detect the sensation and send a message toward the brain (CNS) for processing.

items.title: I can describe the roles of the brain and spinal cord as the two components of the central nervous system
items.what: The brain coordinates mental processes, behaviour, and bodily activity. The spinal cord is a cable of nerve tissue connecting the brain to the PNS via afferent (sensory) tracts that carry messages toward the brain and efferent (motor) tracts that carry messages away from the brain.
items.why: The brain and spinal cord are the processing and routing centre of all neural activity. Knowing the direction of information flow through each structure is essential for describing conscious responses and the spinal reflex.
items.example: When a person decides to pick up a cup, efferent tracts in the spinal cord carry the motor command from the brain down to the muscles of the hand and arm.

items.title: I can describe the role of the somatic nervous system and the neural pathways it contains
items.what: The somatic nervous system (SNS) is a division of the PNS that transmits neural messages related to voluntary motor movement. It contains sensory (afferent) neural pathways made up of sensory neurons that carry messages toward the CNS, and motor (efferent) neural pathways made up of motor neurons that carry messages from the CNS to skeletal muscles.
items.why: The somatic nervous system is the pathway for all voluntary, conscious actions and is directly involved in the spinal reflex. Correctly identifying its role and direction of transmission is a core exam skill.
items.example: A person reaching out to catch a ball uses the somatic nervous system: sensory neurons carry visual and tactile information to the CNS, and motor neurons carry the movement command to the skeletal muscles of the arm.

items.title: I can describe the role of the autonomic nervous system and distinguish between its sympathetic and parasympathetic subdivisions
items.what: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is a division of the PNS that regulates visceral muscles, organs, and glands without conscious control. The sympathetic nervous system activates these structures to prepare the body for a threat or stressor. The parasympathetic nervous system maintains and restores optimal, balanced functioning of these structures.
items.why: The ANS controls the body's internal environment automatically, which explains unconscious physiological responses during stress and rest. Confusing the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions is one of the most common student errors in this topic.
items.example: During a frightening situation, the sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate and dilates pupils. After the threat passes, the parasympathetic nervous system slows the heart rate and restores normal digestion.

items.title: I can identify the three types of neurons and describe the direction in which each transmits neural messages
items.what: Sensory neurons (afferent) transmit messages about bodily sensations from the PNS to the CNS. Motor neurons (efferent) transmit messages about motor movement from the CNS to the PNS. Interneurons transfer messages between sensory and motor neurons and make up the brain and spinal cord.
items.why: Each neuron type has a specific directional role in the nervous system. Knowing which neuron type is found where — and which direction it transmits — is necessary for describing both conscious responses and the spinal reflex accurately.
items.example: In the spinal reflex: sensory neurons carry the pain signal from the skin to the spinal cord; interneurons in the spinal cord relay the signal; motor neurons carry the withdrawal command to the skeletal muscles.

items.title: I can compare the CNS and PNS in terms of the types of neurons each contains
items.what: The CNS — comprising the brain and spinal cord — is made up of interneurons. The PNS is made up of sensory (afferent) neurons and motor (efferent) neurons.
items.why: This comparison is tested directly in VCE multiple-choice and short-answer questions. Students frequently and incorrectly state that the spinal cord contains sensory or motor neurons rather than interneurons.
items.example: A question asks which neurons make up the spinal cord. The correct answer is interneurons, because the spinal cord is part of the CNS — not sensory or motor neurons, which belong to the PNS.
